items.title: Hoe doorbreek je de cirkel van laaggeletterdheid? 7 tips
items.raw_text: Een kind dat er lekker op los kletst, samen met papa en mama boekjes leest en zich goed kan uitdrukken. En ouders die trots toekijken, want hoe anders was hun eigen jeugd… Gezinsgericht werken aan basisvaardigheden levert meer op dan goede ontwikkelkansen. Samen doorbreek je de cirkel van laaggeletterdheid en werk je toe aan meer zelfvertrouwen en zelfredzaamheid. Maar hoe doe je dat als bibliotheekprofessional? Wat is jouw rol? En welke samenwerkingspartners heb je nodig? Dat bespraken we tijdens de Kenniscirkel Gezinsgericht werken aan basisvaardigheden in de Bibliotheek Deventer . Lees in dit artikel 7 inzichten van de deelnemers, die jou verder helpen in je werk. Ervaringen en vraagstukken delen Maar liefst 65 deelnemers waren aanwezig op de Kenniscirkel Gezinsgericht werken aan basisvaardigheden. Onder hen waren specialisten jeugd & educatie, coördinatoren (digi)taalhuizen en projectleiders van de VoorleesExpress. De hoge opkomst laat zien dat er behoefte is aan meer handvatten om gezinsgericht werken aan basisvaardigheden op te pakken. Dat bibliotheken (en samenwerkingspartners) dit onderwerp belangrijk vinden, staat buiten kijf. Hoe ze dit moeten doen en met wie, is voor velen nog een uitdaging. Daarom is het vertrekpunt van de Kenniscirkel ook ‘ervaringen en vraagstukken met elkaar delen’. items.title: Caribische bibliotheken versterken samenwerking tijdens uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador
items.raw_text: Hoe bouw je samen aan een sterk netwerk van bibliotheken, terwijl je ook over grenzen heen van elkaar blijft leren? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens een bijzondere uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador. Bibliotheken uit het Caribisch deel van ons Koninkrijk kwamen samen om kennis en ervaringen met elkaar te delen en om een belangrijke stap te zetten in hun gezamenlijke ontwikkeling. Tijdens de conferentie ondertekenden Biblioteka Nashonal Kòrsou , Biblioteca Nacional Aruba , Biblioteka Públiko Boneiru , Sint Maarten Library , Gertrude Judson Bicentennial Public Library St. Eustatius en Queen Wilhelmina Library hun gezamenlijke netwerkplan. Daarmee bekrachtigen zij hun gedeelde ambities en afspraken voor de komende periode. Een netwerk met ambitie De Caribische bibliotheken werken, met begeleiding van Common Eye , aan een sterk en duurzaam netwerk dat aansluit bij hun eigen behoeften, ervaringen en ambities. Het netwerkplan richt zich onder andere op een sterkere positionering van de Caribische bibliotheken en de ontwikkeling van toekomstbestendige bibliotheken. Als kennis- en expertisepartner zijn wij vanuit Rijnbrink, samen met de Koninklijke Bibliotheek (KB) , betrokken bij het netwerk. We ondersteunen de bibliotheken bij hun organisatorische en inhoudelijke ontwikkeling en helpen mee om de ambities uit het netwerkplan verder te brengen. items.title: Hoe de VoorleesExpress gezinnen versterkt en bibliotheken scherper laat werken
items.raw_text: Thuis, op een vast moment, met een boek in de handen. Dat is de kern van de VoorleesExpress. Al jarenlang werken bibliotheken, vrijwilligers en samenwerkingspartners aan een voorleesritueel bij gezinnen: voor taalplezier, taalontwikkeling én gelijke kansen. Samen bereikten we in Gelderland en Overijssel al meer dan 10.000 gezinnen. Maar door goed te kijken naar wat werkt en wat scherper kan, kunnen we voor méér kinderen en ouders het verschil maken. Hoe voorkom je bijvoorbeeld dat je een deel van de doelgroep mist? En welke gegevens helpen je om de impact zichtbaar te maken? Hiervoor organiseerde Rijnbrink een workshop met het thema ‘Haal meer uit data’, voor VoorleesExpress-projectleiders. In dit artikel vertellen enkele aanwezigen over de waarde van de VoorleesExpress en hoe zij slim gebruikmaken van data. items.title: Prentenboeken in Papiamentu: een feest van herkenning
items.raw_text: Een prentenboek vertalen lijkt eenvoudig: je zet de ene taal om in de andere. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat een kind zich écht herkent in een verhaal? Voor de nieuwe Papiamentu-prentenboeken – gerealiseerd in het project Leesbevordering in meertalige gezinnen – dachten leden van de klankbordgroep mee over taal, cultuur en geschiedenis. Waarom is de keuze voor opa beter dan de officiële vertaling tawela? Waarom mocht het verhaal van Tula in de nieuwe prentenboekencollectie niet ontbreken? En wat gebeurt er als een kind voor het eerst een verhaal in zijn eigen taal hoort? Jakeema, Myrthe en Margriet vertellen hoe juist die keuzes het verschil maken. Waarom vertalen nodig was Zoals het eerdere artikel over dit project al aangaf: voorlezen stimuleert de taalontwikkeling van jonge kinderen het beste. Juist voorlezen in de thuistaal, de taal van het hart, levert veel extra’s op. Ouders op Bonaire willen dat met alle liefde doen, vertelt Jakeema Hernandez, programmaleider bij Bibliotheek Bonaire. Maar de collectie prentenboeken in het Papiamentu is beperkt. Jakeema is dan ook blij met de nieuwe, vertaalde Papiamentu-boeken. Als kind hield ik al van lezen, maar een boek in mijn eigen taal vinden in de boekhandel of bibliotheek was onmogelijk. Voor mijn inner child is het mooi om te zien dat er nu boeken in het Papiamentu bestaan. items.title: Privacy & informatiebeveiliging: dit speelt er in de bibliotheek
items.raw_text: Privacy en informatiebeveiliging zijn belangrijke onderwerpen voor iedere bibliotheek. Maar wat betekenen nieuwe ontwikkelingen nu concreet voor de praktijk? Vanaf nu delen we iedere twee maanden de belangrijkste ontwikkelingen, praktische tips en aandachtspunten voor de bibliotheeksector. In deze eerste editie: nieuwe modeldocumenten voor de Bibliotheek op school, de risico’s en regels rond chatbots en een praktische tip om vandaag nog met informatiebeveiliging aan de slag te gaan. Nieuwe modeldocumenten voor de Bibliotheek op school De modeldocumenten voor de Bibliotheek op school in het primair onderwijs zijn vernieuwd. Dan is het belangrijk om deze direct te vervangen. Deze versies zijn verouderd. Werk je met de model-verwerkersovereenkomst 4.0 uit 2022? Controleer dan of de afspraken nog aansluiten bij de huidige situatie. Bij twijfel is het verstandig om de overeenkomst te vervangen door de nieuwe of herziene versie uit 2026. items.title: Voorlezen in de taal van je hart: meer verhalen in Farsi en Papiamentu
items.raw_text: Een Curaçaos meisje dat glundert als ze het boek ‘Mihó nò’ ontdekt tussen de bibliotheekboeken. Een Iranese vader die een bibliotheekmedewerker speciaal komt bedanken, omdat hij een prentenboek in zijn thuistaal mee kan nemen. Of een Farsi-sprekende moeder die ontroerd raakt, als ze tijdens een bijeenkomst hoort dat dromen en schelden in je thuistaal normaal is. Deze voorbeelden vertellen wat waardering voor thuistalen met mensen doet. Het geeft het gevoel dat jij ertoe doet, dat je verhaal welkom is en dat je je thuis mag voelen. In dit artikel lees je over het project Leesbevordering in meertalige gezinnen. Diverse betrokkenen vertellen wat samen is bereikt en welk doel daarachter zit: álle kinderen laten opgroeien in een stimulerende taalomgeving. Vers van de pers zijn de prentenboeken in Farsi en Papiamentu. Die kunnen bibliotheken sinds half juli bestellen en combineren met meertalige voorleesfilmpjes via de Jeugdbibliotheek en De Voorleeshoek. Ouders en kinderen die samen lezen, luisteren en praten in de taal van hun hart: dáár gaan wij van glunderen! De viering van de Farsi en Papiamentu voorleesfilmpjes met de projectpartners en leesmediaconsulenten uit Bonaire. Praten en voorlezen in de thuistaal? Doen! items.title: Haal meer uit data voor maatschappelijke programmering met de Datateam®methode
items.raw_text: Hoe maak je keuzes rond programmering die niet alleen goed voelen, maar ook goed onderbouwd zijn? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens de inspirerende en energieke workshop Haal meer uit data – De Datateam®methode op 4 juni bij Kunstwerk! in Zevenaar. Dertien bibliotheekmedewerkers uit Gelderland en Overijssel maakten kennis met de Datateam®methode. Universiteit Twente ontwikkelde deze aanpak, die organisaties helpt om maatschappelijke vraagstukken data-geïnformeerd aan te pakken. Onder begeleiding van Maaike Korte (Expertis) ontdekten deelnemers hoe data, samenwerking en een gestructureerde werkwijze kunnen bijdragen aan betere keuzes en sterkere programmering. Benieuwd naar wat deze workshop opleverde? Wij zetten de belangrijkste inzichten voor je op een rijtje. Van vraagstuk naar inzicht Tijdens de interactieve workshop wisselden theorie en praktijk elkaar af. Deelnemers gingen aan de slag met vraagstukken uit hun eigen organisatie. Bijvoorbeeld: hoe bereik je als bibliotheek beter de NT1-doelgroep met je huidige aanbod? In kleine groepen verkenden zij de eerste stappen van de Datateam®methode. Daarbij kregen de deelnemers praktische handvatten om vraagstukken scherper te formuleren, data te verzamelen en samen tot nieuwe inzichten te komen. items.title: HR Actueel – Mogelijke afschaffing compensatie transitievergoeding: wat betekent dit voor bibliotheken?
items.raw_text: Vanaf 2027 ontvangen werkgevers mogelijk geen compensatie meer voor de transitievergoeding bij ontslag wegens langdurige arbeidsongeschiktheid. Dat heeft het kabinet aangekondigd. Hoewel de parlementaire behandeling nog loopt, is het voor bibliotheken en cultuurorganisaties verstandig om nu alvast inzicht te krijgen in de mogelijke gevolgen. Extra kosten bij langdurig verzuim Langdurig verzuim brengt al aanzienlijke kosten met zich mee. Denk aan twee jaar loondoorbetaling, re-integratietrajecten, arbodienstverlening en vervanging van medewerkers. Als de compensatieregeling verdwijnt, komen daar mogelijk ook de kosten van de transitievergoeding volledig bij. De financiële impact kan aanzienlijk zijn. Een medewerker met twintig dienstjaren en een bruto maandsalaris van € 3.500 heeft bijvoorbeeld recht op een transitievergoeding van ruim € 23.000. Zonder compensatie zijn deze kosten volledig voor rekening van de werkgever. Daarmee wordt langdurig verzuim niet alleen een HR-vraagstuk, maar ook een belangrijk onderwerp voor directie, management, begroting en risicomanagement. Aandacht voor slapende dienstverbanden Ook de discussie rondom slapende dienstverbanden kan opnieuw relevanter worden. De compensatieregeling werd destijds ingevoerd om te voorkomen dat werkgevers dienstverbanden na twee jaar ziekte lieten doorlopen om betaling van de transitievergoeding te vermijden. items.title: De tanden in een meerjarenplan
items.raw_text: Elke bibliotheek of MFCO maakt ze: meerjarenbeleidsplannen. Sommigen verheugen zich erop om ermee aan de slag te gaan, anderen vinden het nog best ingewikkeld. Wat moet er precies in? Wat is een goede doelstelling en wie moet je allemaal betrekken? En wat is het verschil tussen een meerjarenbeleidsplan van de bibliotheek en een meerjarenplan van de gemeente in het kader van de zorgplicht? Elk jaar ondersteunt Rijnbrink een flink aantal organisaties in dit proces. Met plezier en met resultaat. De afgelopen periode zetten we samen met de bibliotheek Noord-Veluwe , de bibliotheek Dalfsen en BIJ de bieb de tanden in hun meerjarenplan. In dit artikel lees je hun ervaringen. Meerjarenbeleidsplan Dalfsen: een meerjarenbeleidsplan met paragraaf voor de zorgplicht In Dalfsen hielpen we met een nieuw plan voor de bibliotheek. Bijzonder was dat, naast alle medewerkers, ook de beleidsambtenaar het hele traject heeft meegedaan. Ook waren er verschillende afstemmingsmomenten met samenwerkingspartners. Dat leverde veel lof op. De bibliotheek voegde aan het plan gelijk een paragraaf toe over alle onderdelen die de gemeente mee moet nemen voor de zorgplicht. Jackeline Mekkes, directeur van de Bibliotheek Dalfsen kijkt goed terug op het traject: ‘We hebben nu een goed uitgeschreven meerjarenbeleidsplan en een duidelijke begroting. items.title: 5 inzichten en 10 tips van het Nationale Bibliotheek Congres 2026
items.raw_text: Een recordaantal bibliotheekprofessionals, één gedeelde ambitie: bouwen aan een bibliotheek die voor iedereen van betekenis is. Tijdens het Nationale Bibliotheekcongres op 18 juni 2026 in Utrecht kwamen collega’s uit het hele land samen om kennis te delen, inspiratie op te doen en elkaar te ontmoeten. Onder het thema ‘De Bibliotheek bouwt door: een huis voor iedereen’ spraken zij volop over de rol van bibliotheken in een samenleving die voortdurend verandert. Onder deze ‘reisleiders (geen boekbewakers) in een steeds veranderende wereld’, zoals onze adviseur Anja Annink de aanwezigen omschreef, waren ook veel Rijnbrink-collega’s. Zij volgden sessies, gingen in gesprek met mensen uit het netwerk of leverden zelf een bijdrage aan het programma. De grootste meerwaarde volgens hen? De combinatie van inhoud en ontmoeting. ‘Dit congres helpt ons als sector om elkaar te kennen, van elkaar te leren en gezamenlijk verder te bouwen aan de bibliotheek van de toekomst’, zegt netwerkmanager Tim Trooster. In dit artikel blikken de Rijnbrinkers terug op het congres, dat werd georganiseerd door de KB , de VOB en Stichting SPN . Lees welke inzichten zij er opdeden en met welke tips je als bibliotheek morgen al het verschil kunt maken. items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. Sommigen bepleiten ‘radicale openbaarheid’, wat simpelweg neerkomt op álles openbaar maken. items.title: Veiliginternetten.nl ondersteunt gemeenten om hun inwoners te informeren over online criminaliteit en hoe ze zich daartegen kunnen beschermen
items.raw_text: Hoe bereik je als gemeente inwoners met informatie over online criminaliteit én zorg je dat ze er echt iets mee doen? Hoe bereik je als veiliginternetten.nl iedereen in Nederland met informatie over veilig internetten in de breedste zin van het woord. Dat doe je door samen op te trekken. Gemeenten hoeven het wiel niet zelf uit te vinden. Er zijn al veel goede campagnes en communicatiemiddelen beschikbaar. Op veiliginternetten.nl bieden we verschillende materialen die gemeenten in kunnen zetten om inwoners te informeren. Ook vind je hier de campagnes van het ministerie van Justitie en Veiligheid en het ministerie van Binnenslandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties: ‘Laat je niet interneppen’ en ‘Dubbel beveiligd is dubbel zo veilig’. Tijdens dit webinar zal Sophieke Thurmer toelichten hoe veiliginternetten.nl voorlichters en communicatiespecialisten van gemeenten kan ondersteunen bij hun voorlichting over cybersecurity. Dat kan tijdens de Cybersecuritymaand maar ook op andere inhaakmomenten als de maand van Senioren en Veiligheid (april) en Safer Internet Day in februari. items.title: Vijf tips voor een (nog) betere samenwerking tussen bestuurder en CISO
items.raw_text: Bestuurder en CISO gaan samen invulling geven aan de Cyberbeveiligingswet (Cbw). items.title: Juli
items.raw_text: Online radicalisering van jongeren: het gesprek gaat door Deze maand is er opnieuw veel aandacht voor schadelijke en gewelddadige online netwerken. De NOS berichtte op 23 juli over de aanhouding van een jonge man die wordt verdacht van deelname aan een sadistisch Com-netwerk ofwel community. Binnen dergelijke besloten online groepen kunnen kwetsbare jongeren worden geronseld en aangezet tot zelfbeschadiging, misbruik en geweld. De actuele berichtgeving raakt direct aan de onderwerpen die op 22 juni centraal stonden tijdens het symposium Online radicalisering van jongeren: herkennen, begrijpen en handelen, georganiseerd door de ATKM, de NCTV en ECP. Onder leiding van dagvoorzitter Liesbeth Rasker gingen professionals, onderzoekers en ervaringsdeskundigen in gesprek over de vraag hoe online radicalisering tijdig kan worden herkend, zonder jongeren te snel te veroordelen of te stigmatiseren. Radicalisering begint vaak niet met een uitgesproken ideologie of een duidelijke intentie om geweld te gebruiken. Het kan beginnen bij menselijke vragen: wie ben ik, waar hoor ik bij en wie neemt mij serieus? Online groepen kunnen daarop inspelen en grenzen tussen humor, provocatie, uitsluiting en geweld geleidelijk laten vervagen. De rode draad in het symposium, de podcast en de actuele berichtgeving is daarom dezelfde: blijf nieuwsgierig, investeer in kennis van de online leefwereld en voer het gesprek voordat standpunten en gedrag verder verharden. items.title: Zomerblog Marjolijn Bonthuis
items.raw_text: “Worden we een museum?” Een persoonlijke zomerse beschouwing over Europa, AI en de stap van dialoog naar daadkracht Deze zomer lees ik Grand Hotel Europa van Ilja Leonard Pfeijffer. Het hotel in de roman staat symbool voor Europa: prachtig, rijk aan verhalen, maar vooral gericht op het verleden. Europa bewaart zijn kunst, architectuur en geschiedenis — en verkoopt die aan toeristen. Ondertussen wordt de toekomst elders gebouwd. Die gedachte dringt zich ook op wanneer ik kijk naar de huidige technologische ontwikkelingen. Terwijl Amerikaanse en Chinese bedrijven miljarden investeren in kunstmatige intelligentie, chips en digitale infrastructuur, zijn wij in Europa vaak vooral bezig met regels, risico’s en bescherming. Laat ik daar duidelijk over zijn: die aandacht is nodig. Zeker vanuit mijn dagelijkse verantwoordelijkheid voor digitale veiligheid, weerbaarheid en vertrouwen weet ik hoe belangrijk het is dat technologie niet zonder grenzen wordt ontwikkeld en toegepast. Big Tech heeft inmiddels zoveel economische, technologische en maatschappelijke macht opgebouwd dat stevige publieke kaders onvermijdelijk zijn. Bescherming van grondrechten, democratische controle en eerlijke concurrentie zijn geen luxe. Maar regels alleen maken ons nog geen speler. Als Europa vooral vastlegt onder welke voorwaarden technologie van anderen hier mag worden gebruikt, terwijl we zelf onvoldoende investeren in de ontwikkeling ervan, blijft onze invloed beperkt. items.title: Stichting ECP wijzigt structuur governance om ook in de toekomst bijdrage te kunnen leveren aan de digitale samenleving
items.raw_text: Om waarde te kunnen blijven toevoegen aan de digitale samenleving heeft Stichting ECP haar governance structuur aangepast. Eerder meldde Stichting ECP al dat ze de aanpassing aan het eind van dit jaar wil hebben ingericht, als uitkomst van een traject dat in 2024 in gang is gezet. Stichting ECP is er van overtuigd met deze governance structuur ook in de toekomst haar bijdrage te kunnen leveren via haar activiteiten en in samenwerking met het brede netwerk van publieke en private partijen die zich hiervoor inzetten. Stichting ECP wordt per 1 januari 2027 een zelfstandig opererende organisatie, die zelfstandig activiteiten uitvoert en beheert en worden activiteiten van de verschillende PPS-programma’s en -projecten opnieuw aanbesteed. Een overzicht van wijzigingen governance en inrichting Stichting ECP is aan het einde van dit bericht opgenomen. Met de voorgenomen aanpassingen in de governance structuur zal Stichting ECP uiterlijk 1 januari 2027 voldoen aan de Code Goed Openbaar Bestuur, inclusief de bijbehorende bevoegdheden, besluitvormingsstructuur, benoemingsprocedures- en termijnen en bezoldiging conform WNT, vertaald in de Statuten en het Bestuursreglement. In aanloop naar deze situatie is per 1 juli 2026 de huidige inrichting van de samenwerking tussen Stichting ECP en LunaVia B.V. beëindigd. items.title: Wanneer hulp een weektaak wordt: onderzoek naar informatieplichten in het sociaal domein
items.raw_text: De maatschappelijke coalitie Over Informatie Gesproken De maatschappelijke coalitie Over Informatie Gesproken is een initiatief vanuit ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving. De maatschappelijke coalitie streeft naar een gelijkwaardige informatierelatie tussen burgers en overheid. Een relatie waarin burgers mede-eigenaar zijn van informatie en zodoende bijdragen aan een sterke democratie. Met de call for proposals honoreert de maatschappelijke coalitie elk jaar een aantal onderzoeken die bijdragen aan de informatierelatie tussen burger en overheid. Het onderzoek van Guido Enthoven was een van deze onderzoeken. Voor mensen die te maken hebben met schulden, gezondheidsproblemen, werkloosheid of andere complexe levensomstandigheden kan ondersteuning van de overheid het verschil maken tussen verder in de problemen raken of weer perspectief krijgen. Guido Enthoven (van Instituut Maatschappelijke Innovatie (IMI) laat in zijn onderzoek Klem in het systeem. Informatieplichten voor multiprobleemhuishoudens zien hoe ingewikkeld de administratieve werkelijkheid inmiddels is geworden voor mensen rond de armoedegrens. Het onderzoek richt zicht op Rotterdam-Zuid waar relatief veel mensen een minimuminkomen hebben. items.title: Van systeemwereld naar leefwereld
items.raw_text: Vanuit publieke waarden vormgeven aan digitale transitie Digitaal Doordacht als vertrekpunt Binnen het programma Digitaal Doordacht werken het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) en ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving samen aan een toekomstgerichte overheid waarin burgers en ondernemers centraal staan. Met een reeks veranderverhalen maken we zichtbaar waar het écht kantelt: waar professionals elkaar vinden, aannames ter discussie komen en keuzes ontstaan die versnelling én borging mogelijk maken. We werken in korte cycli van ophalen, duiden en verbinden, met strategische verankering en blijvende aandacht voor ethiek, privacy en security. Zo wordt digitalisering geen abstracte belofte, maar een reeks concrete interventies die adoptie, vertrouwen en maatschappelijke impact versnellen. Peter van Waart: AI als maatschappelijke opgave In dit veranderverhaal staat Peter van Waart centraal, Human Experience Design Researcher en bij Hogeschool Rotterdam werkzaam als programmamanager Smart & Social City. Zijn verhaal laat zien hoe publieke innovatie ontstaat op het snijvlak van strategie en uitvoering. items.raw_text: Het Nederland Digitaal Festival, bent u erbij? Op woensdag 18 en donderdag 19 november 2026 vindt de allereerste editie plaats van het Nederland Digitaal Festival (het nieuwe ECP Jaarfestival) georganiseerd door ECP en SIDN. Een onafhankelijk event waar alle relevante partijen in onze digitale samenleving samenkomen om gezamenlijk richting te geven aan de digitale toekomst van Nederland. We versturen binnenkort de save the date, wilt u deze ontvangen, laat dan uw gegevens achter! Laat hier uw gegevens achter ‘Digitale soevereiniteit vraagt niet om alleen meer beleid, maar om beter politiek leiderschap en experimenteren’ Tijdens het symposium ‘Digitale economie en soevereiniteit – uitdagingen en handelingsperspectief’ gingen vertegenwoordigers uit overheid, bedrijfsleven, wetenschap, politiek en maatschappelijke organisaties met elkaar in gesprek over het versterken van de digitale weerbaarheid van Nederland en Europa. Het werd duidelijk dat digitale soevereiniteit niet alleen draait om technologie, maar vooral om investeren, samenwerken en durven kiezen. items.title: Building Leadership Through Associations: A Conversation with Loida Garcia-Febo
items.raw_text: How can library associations strengthen leadership and help library and information professionals respond to increasingly complex and uncertain environments? On 25 June 2026, Loida Garcia-Febo, Chair of the IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) , joined a conversation with Roxana Huaman Huriarte, Chair of the IFLA Latin America and the Caribbean Regional Division , and Nick Boxem, Chair of the IFLA Europe Regional Division , both members of the IFLA Regional Council leadership group. The conversation explored leadership within IFLA and library associations, and how strategic planning, capacity building and professional networks can help organisations and individuals respond more effectively to change. Leadership is a capacity that can be developed Leadership is not simply linked to holding a formal position but it is a capacity that can be intentionally developed through experience, training, mentoring, coaching and opportunities to work with others. For library associations, this means creating environments where current and emerging leaders can learn, test ideas, build confidence and develop the skills required to guide organisations through change. Garcia-Febo highlighted the importance of leadership training, mentoring and coaching, alongside team building and effective communication. items.title: Construyendo liderazgo a través de las asociaciones: Una conversación con Loida Garcia-Febo
items.raw_text: ¿Cómo pueden las asociaciones bibliotecarias fortalecer el liderazgo y ayudar a los bibliotecarios y profesionales de la información a responder a entornos cada vez más complejos e inciertos? El 25 de junio de 2026, Loida Garcia-Febo, Chair de la Sección de Gestión de Asociaciones de Bibliotecarios de IFLA (MLAS) , participó en una conversación con Roxana Huaman Huriarte, Chair de la División Regional de América Latina y el Caribe de IFLA , y Nick Boxem, Chair de la División Regional de Europa de IFLA , ambos miembros del grupo de liderazgo del Consejo Regional de IFLA. La conversación exploró el liderazgo dentro de IFLA y de las asociaciones bibliotecarias, así como la manera en que la planificación estratégica, el fortalecimiento de capacidades y las redes profesionales pueden ayudar a las organizaciones y a las personas a responder de manera más efectiva al cambio. El liderazgo es una capacidad que puede desarrollarse El liderazgo no está simplemente vinculado a ocupar una posición formal, sino que es una capacidad que puede desarrollarse intencionalmente a través de la experiencia, la formación, la mentoría, el coaching y las oportunidades para trabajar con otros. Para las asociaciones bibliotecarias, esto significa crear entornos en los que los líderes actuales y emergentes puedan aprender, poner a prueba ideas, desarrollar confianza y adquirir las habilidades necesarias para guiar a las organizaciones a través del cambio. items.title: IFLA Europe Regional Division Webinar 2026: How EURDC supports Libraries across Europe
items.raw_text: The IFLA Europe Regional Division invites library professionals, information specialists, and IFLA members from across Europe to an engaging online webinar on 1 October 2026 at 11:00 CEST . Over the past five years, the Europe Regional Division Committee (EURDC) has worked to strengthen collaboration, advocacy, and engagement among libraries and library professionals throughout Europe. Despite these efforts, many colleagues remain unfamiliar with the division’s mandate, activities, and opportunities for involvement. This webinar aims to change that. During the session, four members of the current EURDC Committee, representing Finland, Germany, Norway, and Portugal, will introduce the division’s work and share practical examples of how EURDC supports the European library community. Participants will gain insights into the division’s objectives, ongoing initiatives, and future priorities. The webinar will also provide an opportunity for dialogue. Attendees will be encouraged to share their expectations, discuss challenges facing libraries in Europe, and suggest ways in which EURDC can better support their work and professional communities. The event will be conducted in English via Zoom, with automated subtitles available to improve accessibility. Event Details Date: 1 October 2026 Time: 11:00 CEST Format: Online (Zoom) Language: English Register Now

items.title: The Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) WLIC 2026 Outcomes Report
items.raw_text: Part of MLAS Members and Attendees at MLAS Business Meeting in Busan The IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) had an active and substantive presence at the IFLA World Library and Information Congress (WLIC) 2026 in Busan. Activities included the MLAS Business Meeting, MLAS Open Session, IFLA Associations Meeting, an informal meeting of International Relations Chairs, and opportunities for congress attendees to connect with the MLAS Chair at the IFLA exhibition booth. Across these activities, common priorities emerged: strategic renewal, member engagement, leadership, partnerships, advocacy, financial sustainability, visibility, digital transformation and AI, resilience, crisis preparedness, and responsiveness to changing societal needs. These priorities are closely aligned with MLAS’s mission to support strong, well-managed library associations through leadership, peer learning, resource development, and effective association practices worldwide. Strong library associations do not simply have strategies. They make their strategies visible, translate them into action, engage their members, build partnerships, advocate effectively, develop new leaders, sustain their organisations, and continually renew themselves in response to change. items.title: IFLA President’s Message – August 2026
items.raw_text: The below message has been distributed to IFLA members and volunteers in all IFLA languages. I am writing to you today, still trying to get my feet back on the ground after an amazing time at our World Library and Information Congress in Busan . This was my first time attending as President! I will admit that I lost count of the number of meetings, speeches and other events I was involved in, but know that each one reinforced my excitement about libraries and our Federation. I will also admit to some pride in my gong technique. I want to begin by highlight the incredible winners of our awards this year, as well as our IFLA Medal and Scroll of Appreciation recipients. Thank you for all you do in support of libraries, our profession and IFLA. It was inspiring to see the extent to which political decision-makers in Korea both understand the potential of libraries and support libraries in realizing their potential. It is a situation we can all aspire to! It was such a pleasure to have an opportunity to talk individually with so many of you attending the Congress, whether members, volunteers or stakeholders, to thank you for your incredible support and friendship. I am sorry that I couldn’t connect personally with everyone, but I do hope that you are already putting our Congress next year in London in your diaries. items.title: The Great IFLA100 Futures Challenge
items.raw_text: Join us on the first stage of our drive to engage the global library field in a reflection on the future(s) of our institutions, our place in society, and our international cooperation. A key pillar of the programme for IFLA’s centenary year – IFLA100 – is a focus on the future. Alongside the remembering and celebration of our past achievements and the people that made them possible, we want this year to be a chance to build up the skills, attitudes and connections necessary to enter into our second century with confidence. Central to this is our work to build up the habit of futures thinking across our profession. This enables us to steer a path between a denialism driven by passivity, and an excessive reliance on specific predictions that leaves little room to react to the unexpected. IFLA already has a strong record of work in this space. Our Trend Report in 2024 shared a set of potential trends, as well as using these to offer a range of potential scenarios for the future, ready to be used by libraries and library workers to test their own plans. Our Weak Signals report added to this, using ideas gathered at the 2025 World Library and Information Congress to identify phenomena that could potentially have a transformative effect in the future. At our 2026 Congress, the keynote speech by Sohail Inayatullah provided further insights into techniques for futures thinking, complementing the keynote given by Riel Miller at our Toronto meetings in April. items.title: Call for Proposals: Consultancy on International Association Membership, Volunteer and Congress Models
items.raw_text: IFLA is looking for a consultant that can support work to ensure that our membership, volunteer and Congress financial models are optimised as we enter our second century, drawing on insights and best practice from peer organisations. This work takes place as part of our Sustainable Futures Journey, which brings together a range of initiatives intended to strengthen our Federation’s ability to deliver on its current and future strategies. The work on reviews of our membership, volunteer and congress financial models is being led by members of our Governing Board, with a strong emphasis on engaging our communities and partners, and drawing on their experience and ideas. At the same time, we are realistic about the fact that there are many other international associations which face similar situations to our own, and which can offer us valuable lessons and ideas to inform our own work. This is where we are seeking a consultant who can support the work of our Board by bringing together key examples and inputs. Details of our expectations are set out in the formal call , which is open until 15 September. We welcome applications from around the world, and from teams of consultants.

items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.raw_text: Welcome to American Libraries’ 2026 Library Design Showcase, our annual celebration of new and renovated libraries across the US and Canada. The word welcome appeared in many of this year’s submissions, reflecting a growing understanding that in anxious times, the library is a place that should feel good: safe, comfortable, well-lit, plugged in, and deeply connected to its surroundings. More than two-thirds of this year’s 15 selections are renovations or adaptive reuse projects. Libraries of all types are finding ways to acknowledge historical and environmental realities, embrace natural elements and cultural identities, evolve traditions, and build in flexibility to account for the unexpected. Read on for snapshots of these communities in motion. Natural immersion Maplewood (N.J.) Memorial Library Adjacent to a historic park, with protected natural areas on all sides, this 1955 masonry structure had nowhere to expand but up. The new, light-filled second floor features bird-safe glass, wood battens, and green roofs for a treehouse feel. The all-electric building, the first LEED Gold–certified library in New Jersey, includes solar panels that offset more than half of the library’s energy use. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.title: Newsmaker: Min Jin Lee
items.raw_text: Min Jin Lee has notched career milestones that few authors reach. Her immigration saga Pachinko was both a National Book Award finalist and a New York Times Top 10 Best Book of 2017, and it was adapted into a television series of the same name for Apple TV. Lee is also a Guggenheim fellow and the first Korean American to hold the role of New York State author laureate. Her latest title, American Hagwon (Cardinal, September), examines the influence of Korean “cram schools” among families in the Korean diaspora. American Libraries spoke with Lee ahead of her appearance at the American Library Association’s 2026 Annual Conference and Exhibition in Chicago. She discussed her new book, the library that shaped her, and her antidote to book bans. What inspired you to focus on the education system as it relates to the movements of a middle-class Korean American family in American Hagwon ? My research process involved all these interviews—I’ve done hundreds of them, probably almost 1,000 at this point—and every single time I talked to somebody, they would mention their education path. It was such an important and controversial subject. I thought, if I had to think about the most important value for Koreans, especially in the diaspora, what would I write about? Education turned out to be a beast, because people have lots of feelings about it. In the book, the Koh family loses wealth and status as they weather betrayal and financial crises. items.title: Mall Wonder
items.raw_text: After serving its community for nearly 45 years in the same building, Escondido (Calif.) Public Library closed in April 2025 for an $11.6 million renovation. It was important to us, as the city’s lone library, to preserve access during construction. So one month later, our library opened a temporary location in a very different kind of facility: the nearby North County Mall, where services and collections were spread across six storefronts, including a former Abercrombie & Fitch clothing store. Of course, moving a library takes more than a month. Our planning took more than a year and required staff to work under tight deadlines, limited budgets, and high expectations. Here’s how we did it, and what we learned from the process. Choosing a location. It’s essential to consider whether the new location will match, improve upon, or limit access. Retailers and mall operators have already studied traffic patterns, visibility, parking, and nearby amenities. Leverage that knowledge to evaluate access. In our case, the public benefited from a highway and bus stop near the mall, and adjacency to a city park. The arrangement also gave the mall a stable civic tenant and created natural cross-traffic between library patrons and shoppers. The mall was not just available space; it was a location where public access, economic development, and community visibility could overlap. items.title: Dismantling Disinformation
items.raw_text: Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive. Book Bans, Disinformation, and Cultural Erasure: The Censor­ship Movement in Libraries, Schools, and Society By Paul T. Jaeger Jaeger situates the current book-banning movement within a larger social and political effort to erase marginalized communities and culture. He provides clear definitions and examples of these processes and goals, including the roles played by technological progress and economic inequity. With accessible references (like the Beatles, Dungeons & Dragons, and Holmes and Watson) and nuanced examinations of McCarthyism, the history of libraries, and the myth of neutrality, this is a recommended read for anyone interested in a more expansive understanding of current First Amendment challenges. Bloomsbury Libraries Unlimited, 2026. 320 p. $31.50. 979-8-216-39714-4. (Also available as an ebook.) items.title: A Sense of Purpose
items.raw_text: When it comes to building resilient and equitable communities, libraries are natural leaders. We provide places where neighbors meet, learn, and support one another; where sustainability education becomes action; and where residents can find year-round climate refuge. When communities are resilient, they are better able to overcome barriers. The Obama Presidential Center (OPC) branch of Chicago Public Library (CPL) is an example of a library that strengthens the social infrastructure that underpins resilience. CPL Commissioner Chris Brown describes the branch as a civic platform for residents, artists, educators, and organizations to cocreate the life of the library and its surrounding public spaces. Though just 5,000 square feet, OPC was designed to spark connection, invite conversation, and inspire activities that encourage ­socialization and enjoyment. The branch partners with such nonprofits as the Art Institute of Chicago, the literary arts group StoryStudio Chicago , and the artist-led alt_Chicago . OPC is a striking example of how libraries do not just serve resilient communities, they help create them. On the Gulf Coast, sustainability is a daily requirement. Lindsay Cronk, dean of Tulane University Libraries in New Orleans, has shared that the library’s partnership with Keep Louisiana Beautiful , a state program, helps connect students, faculty, and staff with opportunities for conservation, beautification, recycling, and environmental action. items.title: Now Available: Clarivate Releases Pulse of the Library 2026 Survey Report
items.raw_text: From Clarivate : Clarivate today released the Pulse of the Library 2026 report. Now in its third year, the global survey examines how libraries are responding to technological change, including AI, shifting priorities and growing demands on staff and resources. The findings reveal that Mainland China recorded the highest level of AI implementation, with 28% reporting moderate to active implementation, more than double the rate in 2024 and well above the 16% global figure. The report also shows a widening gap between libraries moving beyond experimentation with AI and those still in the earliest stages of AI adoption. 51% of libraries in active implementation operate under joint library and IT governance, against 26% of the sample overall, signaling the importance of structured governance models and interdepartmental collaboration. Oren Beit-Arie, Senior Vice President, Strategy & Innovation, Academia & Government at Clarivate, said: “For libraries, AI marks a continuous shift along with a set of hard choices about when to adopt, when to hold back and how to protect academic integrity and library core values. What stands out in this year’s research are the differences between libraries choosing to experiment, learn and build confidence with AI and those taking a wait-and-see approach, whether by choice or because resources are limited.” Other key findings from the report include: Concerns are evolving as implementation advances. items.title: New Freckle Project Report Examines 15 Years of Public Library Use
items.raw_text: From EveryLibrary Institute: A new Freckle Project Report, “15 Years of IMLS Figures” , looks at national public library statistics from 2010 through 2024 and identifies a striking contrast: American public libraries have more facilities, more staff, and higher levels of funding than at any point in the period examined, while several major measures of physical library use remain substantially below their 2010 levels. The Freckle Project is led by researcher Tim Coates, and its publication is supported by the EveryLibrary Institute. The August 2026 Report examines 15 years of data from the Institute of Museum and Library Services on America’s public libraries. In 2024, the United States had 17,580 public library facilities and 147,289 library employees, while public libraries received nearly $18 billion for operations and another $1.6 billion for capital expenditures. Yet annual visits declined from approximately 1.57 billion in 2010 to 869 million in 2024, while total circulation fell from approximately 2.47 billion to 1.71 billion. Coates’s analysis highlights an especially significant decline in adult physical circulation. After subtracting electronic and children’s circulation from total circulation, he estimates that this category fell approximately 68 percent between 2010 and 2024. items.raw_text: The article linked below was published by Public Library Quarterly. Title Accountability, Integrity: AI Policy in Public Libraries Authors Kathryn FitzGerald University of Washington Benjamin Lee University of Washington Source Public Library Quarterly DOI: 1 0.1080/01616846.2026.2725502 Abstract As artificial intelligence reshapes both library work and the information environment, public libraries must determine whether or how to engage with AI while maintaining library values. To our knowledge, there exists no published analysis of how American and Canadian public library AI policies might link library values and technology adoption. To address this gap, we conducted an environmental scan of public library websites to identify and analyze AI policy statements. Our scan of over 200 library websites identified 32 AI polcies. All reference at least two values, with privacy, security, and responsibility the most frequently cited. items.title: Report: The Federal Program Keeping Libraries Online? the FCC Might Gut It
items.raw_text: From the Indianapolis Star: Under the atrium at the Indianapolis Public Library , a woman is busily typing away on her laptop. Another patron seated at the Central Branch is charging their device while streaming music through earbuds as they read quietly between the stacks. Free Wi-Fi allows Hoosiers a cozy and safe place to access the internet at all 26 library locations across Indianapolis. Potential cuts, however, by the Federal Communications Commission have put that access at risk, advocates warn, and not just in Indiana, but for millions of people in libraries and public schools across the country. The FCC recently put into question whether a 30-year-old program that helps keep libraries online should be changed, left alone, or end. No decisions have been reached, but librarians are concerned about what it could mean for their funding. In late June, the FCC issued what appeared to be a benign notice addressing child safety under one of its service operations. Buried within the 86-page document were eight words that sent shockwaves among librarians and educators alike: “Should the E-Rate program be limited or sunset?” [Clip] “This definitely caught us by surprise,” said Jamar Rahming , president-elect of the Public Library Association and CEO of Cuyahoga County Public Library in Cleveland, Ohio. “E-Rate has been just such a fixture in our public library institutions and communities.” Learn More, Read the Complete Article (about 2300 words) The post Report: The Federal Pr

items.title: Association of American Publishers (AAP) and The Authors Guild Release New Study Analyzing the Impact of Library E-Lending on Commercial Book Markets
items.raw_text: From a Joint Release: Today, the Association of American Publishers (AAP) and the Authors Guild announced the release of a landmark independent study by leading economists at Secretariat Advisors, titled An Empirical Study of the Impact of Library E-Lending on the Book Economy. The study, commissioned jointly by AAP and the Authors Guild, but independently conducted by Secretariat Advisors’ economists, provides the most rigorous analysis to date of how the steep shift toward digital lending in recent years has affected the commercial marketplace for books in the United States, specifically, the consumer sales on which authors and publishers rely for financial success. The research concludes that increased digital access to e-books through library apps influences consumer behavior and impacts commercial markets across both physical and digital formats. The study further concludes there is robust and economically meaningful evidence of direct substitution between library e-lending and retail sales and that decreases in library e-book prices or certain other changes to licensing terms, as required in recent state legislative initiatives, would cause further harm to commercial markets. Authors, publishers, and libraries enjoy a close relationship and shared objective to promote and maximize reading across all levels of society, not only to champion established works of literature but to support the continued production of books not yet written. items.raw_text: Acknowledgments: The author thanks Hayley Park of the University of Maryland for her contributions to language used in this article and Derek Wilmott of the University of Toledo for his assistance in developing the incident reporting form. Libraries across the country are navigating heightened immigration enforcement activity while trying to support community members and staff. Library leaders may face difficult decisions about how to respond to enforcement activity, address harassment, communicate with their communities, and protect patrons and employees, often with limited information about what other libraries are experiencing. Consider a public library responding to increased immigration enforcement activity in its community. Library leadership might consider issuing a public statement supporting immigrants but ultimately decide against it after consulting legal counsel, concerned that doing so could make the library a target. How can library leaders make decisions like this when much of the information available to them comes from anecdotal experiences or informal conversations with colleagues? Better data can help. items.title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. Yet when she begins rehearsing with her fellow contestants, Taryn must confront the challenge of collaborating and competing with contestants whose success could mean her death. items.title: Autism Acceptance at All Ages
items.raw_text: Autism acceptance efforts have come a long way in recent years, and libraries are one of the key reasons why. As a librarian and the mother of two sons with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), I’ve witnessed this progress firsthand. In my capacity as the assistant director of the Beals Memorial Library (BML), I’ve seen how efforts to create more inclusive programs, services, and spaces can promote positive social change that dra-matically improves people’s quality of life, disabled or not. Through our “See Beyond the Spectrum” initiative, in recent years, BML has established new ASD-friendly programs, made our existing programs more accessible, updated our collections with texts by autistic writers, and established an autism caregiver support group. Our staff have gone through autism awareness training, and we’ve established partnerships with local organizations that serve autistic youth. Much of this workhas been supported by external grants, including generous funding from the ALA’s “Libraries Transforming Communities” initiative, which seeks to help libraries become more accessible to patrons with disabilities. Everything we’ve done has proved beneficial, both inside and outside of the library. Staff-patron interactions are more productive and less awkward. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. New chapter leaders can request a starter kit complete with stickers and bookmarks mailed directly to them. items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content. items.title: One Year Later: The Digital Equity Act Cancellation and Libraries
items.raw_text: May 8, 2026, marked the one-year anniversary of the Trump Administration’s cancellation of the Digital Equity Act (DEA). The $2.75 billion Digital Equity Act was a part of a coordinated effort to provide communities across the U.S. with high-speed broadband and the skills and technology needed to thrive in our increasingly digital world. Libraries and other community anchor institutions were integral to the planning of this once-in-a-generation opportunity to address the digital divide. Collectively, these groups spent precious resources and staff time applying for DEA program grants, leading related coalition building efforts, and conducting outreach and asset mapping. The abrupt cancellation of the DEA grants last year was a significant blow to digital inclusion programs nationwide, impacting millions of Americans. According to the Idaho Commission for Libraries , over 80% of the state’s DEA Capacity Grant award “was slated for subgrants supporting rural Idahoans, including older adults and veterans.” Public and tribal libraries across the state would have benefited from grants to replace outdated computers to offer public training on cybersecurity and technology use. In Maine, nearly 130,000 people would have been directly served by DEA-funded programs, such as digital skills training, technical support, telehealth access, and affordable device programs. items.raw_text: Rennie McDougall ‘s Nonstop Bodies: How Dance Shaped New York City gives readers a thrilling new perspective on twentieth century New York City by investigating the different choreographers, dancers, and dance movements that flourished there during that time. McDougall guides the reader through various dance movements, from the marathon dances of the Prohibition era to the Lindy Hop to the Rockettes and beyond. All the while, he catalogues the dense web of lineages that developed among specific dances and artists, allowing readers to see relationships among disparate dance forms that might not be immediately apparent. McDougall also dives into how social and historical forces directly molded the evolving dance forms, and the unique position New York City held to create countless connections between dancers and choreographers not only in the moment, but across time as well. Critics have heaped praise on the book, with Library Journal hailing it as “a love song to dance in all its forms and the city that invented and perfected so many styles.” McDougall spoke with us about taking a different approach to dance history, bringing readers into the immediacy of dancing, and how the texture of the dancers’ lives unconsciously affected the evolution of dance. items.raw_text: ULC, PLA, CULC/CBUC, COSLA, ARSL, seek sustainable pricing for digital access for all readers As community demand continues to ramp up, organizations representing the vast majority of North American public libraries today released a joint statement calling for change in licensing for digital content. The explosion in usage is straining public library budgets and dragging down wait lists for readers in ways that are not sustainable. While libraries are able to purchase physical books and lend them indefinitely, digital content is typically licensed to libraries for a limited time, check-out limit, or both. And, while consumers pay $13 for an e-book on average, libraries typically spend magnitudes more for a two-year license, often $55 or more. “Publishers, authors, and public libraries should be partners, but with the exponential growth in digital content demand, libraries are unable to provide and sustain access under current licensing models. The moment is ripe for large publishers to meet with libraries across North America, to hear our concerns, and address them, so we can continue building a mutually beneficial future for literacy and reading.” — Brooks Rainwater, President and CEO, Urban Libraries Council (ULC) “America’s public libraries are critical to digital discovery of authors and titles, as well as literacy builders and champions.
